creative.body:
My constipation got so bad I considered driving myself to the ER. It gave me terrifying bleeding hemorrhoids one day and left me so backed up by the next that I genuinely thought my colon was going to rupture.

I'm 54. I'd been on Wegovy for 5 months. And what I figured out in the 72 hours after that night is the reason I am writing this.

I had lost 31 pounds. The most I had ever lost in my life. My knees stopped hurting. My A1C dropped almost a full point. My husband pulled out a pair of jeans I had not worn in 9 years and they fit. People at church started asking what I was doing.

Everything was working except 1 thing.

I had stopped going to the bathroom.

7 days. 9 days. Once, 11. By month 4 there were 6 different products on my bathroom counter and I had already been to the ER once and been sent home with a stronger prescription.

What I am about to tell you happened over 72 hours.

Wednesday morning, 7:14am.

I sat down on the toilet and the bleeding started. There was nothing in there to come out. My body was tearing itself trying. I bled into the bowl for the better part of 20 minutes. I cried sitting there.

I cleaned myself up and went to the kitchen. My husband was making coffee. I did not tell him.

I went to work.

I sat at my desk all day with a heating pad against my lower back and pretended I was fine. I did not eat lunch. I came home at 5pm and unbuttoned my jeans before I sat down on the couch.

Wednesday night, 10pm.

My abdomen had become a brick.

I could press 4 fingers into it and they would not give. I could not breathe deeply. The pressure under my ribs was sharp enough that I caught my breath every time I shifted on the couch. I stood up to walk to the bedroom and the weight of my own torso pulling on my back made me dizzy.

I did not lie down in the bed.

I went to the recliner in the living room with a pillow under my knees and slept sitting up. Lying flat made it worse. My husband came down at midnight to find me sitting in the recliner with my eyes open and the TV off. He asked what was wrong. I told him my stomach hurt.

That was as close to the truth as I could get out loud.

Thursday, all day.

13 days.

13 days without a bowel movement.

I drank water. I could not eat. I tried to. I made myself a piece of toast at 9am and looked at it and put it back in the cabinet. The thought of putting more food on top of what was already trapped inside me made me lightheaded.

I went to work again. I sat at my desk again. My husband texted me at 2pm and asked if I had eaten. I told him I had. I had not.

I came home and tried to sleep in the recliner again. I could not. I watched the clock turn from 9 to 10 to 11.

Friday, 11pm. The ER parking lot.

I drove myself to the emergency room.

I parked in the visitor lot and put my hand on the door handle of my own car and could not open it.

I sat there for 40 minutes.

I had Googled "impacted bowel" twice on the drive over. I knew where this was going. I knew what they were going to do. I knew it was going to involve a tube and a room and a stranger explaining to a 54-year-old woman that her body had gotten so backed up that they needed to manually evacuate her.

I could not make myself walk through those sliding doors and tell a triage nurse I was 54 years old, on a weight loss medication, and I had not had a bowel movement in 13 days.

I sat in the parking lot and watched 2 ambulances come in and 1 leave. I watched a woman walk in holding her arm against her chest. I watched a man in scrubs come outside to smoke a cigarette.

I Googled "impacted bowel" a third time and read the symptoms again, the way you reread a paragraph hoping it will say something different.

It did not.

I drove home.

I drove the 22 minutes home with both hands on the wheel and tears on my face and a brick in my abdomen and a phrase running on a loop in my head, which was that I had just chosen to be afraid of a hospital more than I was afraid of my own colon rupturing in my recliner.

That was the moment something in me broke open.

Saturday, 1am. The kitchen table.

I did not go to the recliner when I got home. I sat down at my kitchen table with my phone and a glass of water.

I started reading.

The first 2 hours, all I did was scroll the GLP-1 forums on Reddit. I searched the words I had said out loud to myself in the parking lot. "13 days." "Bleeding." "Brick." "ER."

Other women had said the exact same words. Out loud, into a thread, with their real screen names attached.

A woman in Ohio writing at 3am on her 14th day. A woman in Texas describing the pressure under her ribs by 4pm in the same words I had used to my husband. A woman my age in Phoenix who had also turned around in an ER parking lot 6 weeks earlier.

I read for 2 hours and I cried the entire time, not because of the pain, but because I had spent 5 months thinking I was the only woman in America with a body this broken.

Saturday, 4am. The gastric motility forum.

I clicked a link inside one of those Reddit threads and ended up on a forum I had never heard of, run by people who actually treat motility disorders.

The first thread on the page was titled, "Why your GLP-1 patient does not need another colon laxative."

That was the first time I saw the word "stomach" instead of "colon."

I read that thread until the sun came up.

I made a pot of coffee at 6am Saturday and slept for 3 hours on the couch and went back to the kitchen table at 11am.

Sunday afternoon. Pieced it together.

I sat at my kitchen table with everything I had read and started writing it out for myself in my own words, because I needed to hear it in my own voice before I would believe it.

The medication works in 2 places. Not 1.

The appetite suppression, the part that makes you eat less, that happens in your brain. That is the engine of the weight loss. That is why I had lost 31 pounds. That part was doing exactly what it was supposed to do. I did not want to undo it.

But there is a second thing the medication does.

It takes your stomach from normal to nearly frozen. Food that should leave the stomach in 4 hours sits there for 10. 12. Sometimes 14. And while it sits there, bacteria ferment it.

That is where every symptom I had been suffering through was coming from.

The bloating. The constipation. The hemorrhoids. The brick in my abdomen by 4pm. The 13-day stretches. The ER parking lot.

All of it. Coming from my stomach. Not my colon.

I sat at my kitchen table at 2pm and pictured it.

Stomach at the top. 6 feet of intestine in between. Then the colon at the bottom. The food was sitting at the top. The bacteria were fermenting at the top. The bloating was starting at the top.

Miralax. Colace. Magnesium. Fiber gummies. Probiotics. Psyllium husk. Prune juice.

Every single product on my bathroom counter worked at the bottom.

6 feet downstream from where the actual problem was sitting.

I had been treating the wrong organ for 5 months.

Miralax pulls water into the colon. There was nothing in my colon to pull water into. The food was still trapped 6 feet upstream. That is why it worked while I took it and why the second I stopped, I was right back where I started.

And every week I kept taking it, my body was forgetting how to move on its own.

I needed something that worked on the stomach itself. Not the colon.

I went looking for it. I found apigenin. A plant compound concentrated in celery juice. It works on the smooth muscle of the stomach wall, gently helping the contractions start again. Not a laxative. Not a stimulant. Not a dependency. And critically, it does not override the medication. The brain part, the engine of the weight loss, is not touched. Apigenin only works on the stomach side effect.

I read about chlorophyllin, which binds the sulfur compounds the bacteria are producing in your stalled stomach, neutralizing the bloating and the burps at the source.

I read about a small targeted dose of soluble prebiotic fiber for the lower gut once the upstream is moving again. Not bulk-forming. Not Metamucil. Grams, not handfuls.

The dose research called for 30 to 50mg of standardized apigenin extract. Most celery capsules on Amazon are 500mg of celery powder, which contains less than 0.1% apigenin by weight. A woman buying 1 of those is taking less than 1 milligram a day. Less than 1/30th of what the studies used.

A capsule needs a working stomach to dissolve. If your stomach is the problem, a capsule is the wrong delivery. The version that actually reaches a slowed stomach is pre-dissolved.

Sunday, 6pm. I ordered Motilli.

Heart-shaped gummies. Standardized apigenin extract from celery, not powder. Chlorophyllin and a small targeted dose of soluble prebiotic. 90-day money-back guarantee. Small-batch because apigenin degrades from light and heat. 2 a day.

I closed my phone and ate dinner at the kitchen table for the first time in 4 days.

The first 4 days on the bottle, nothing. By the end of the first week the pressure under my ribs by 4pm was less sharp. The second week I went on my own for the first time in over a month. I sat on the edge of the tub afterward and could not remember the last time my body had done that without me forcing it.

By week 6 I had taken the Miralax, the Colace, the magnesium citrate, the fiber gummies, and the psyllium husk off the counter and put them in a trash bag. My husband walked in and saw the empty counter and said, "Took you long enough."

I have not been back to an ER. I have not had bleeding hemorrhoids. The brick in my abdomen is gone.

If you are sitting in an ER parking lot at 11pm right now and you cannot make yourself walk in, please read what I read that weekend.

You do not have to spend 72 hours like I did. I already spent them.

The mechanism is simple once you find it.

The medication works in 2 places. Brain part is the engine of your weight loss. Don't undo it. Stomach part is the side effect. Every symptom is coming from there. Every product on every shelf works 6 feet downstream. Apigenin works on the right organ.

If you have a vacation, a holiday, a wedding coming up, I would not wait until next week. The bottles sell out for stretches.
